title: The Lesson I Learned From “Follow Me”
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From “Follow Me”
The Two Words That Exposed Everything I Thought I Knew About Jesus
There are moments in Scripture that feel less like reading and more like being read.
Moments when a single sentence reaches through centuries, slips past our defenses, and quietly asks us a question we have spent our entire lives avoiding.
For me, that moment was not a miracle.
It was not the parting of the sea.
It was not the resurrection account.
It was two simple words spoken by Jesus:
Yet those two words changed fishermen into apostles, tax collectors into evangelists, persecutors into preachers, and broken sinners into living testimonies of God's grace.
And if we are honest, they still have the power to change us today.
The first time Jesus spoke these words in the Gospel accounts, He approached ordinary men living ordinary lives.
“And he saith unto them, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.” (Matthew 4:19)
The Greek text records Jesus saying:
Not merely believe facts about Me.
A disciple does not lead Jesus.
Yet so much of modern Christianity attempts the opposite.
We ask Jesus to follow our plans.
But Jesus never invited anyone to place Him behind their life.
He invited them to place Him ahead of it.
That realization hit me harder than I expected.
Because I discovered I had spent years believing in Jesus while still trying to remain in control.
And control is often the last idol to die.
The lesson became even clearer when I studied the encounter between Jesus and Peter after the resurrection.
But they are haunted by their failures.
They secretly wonder whether God can still use someone like them.
Then comes one of the most beautiful moments in all of Scripture.
Notice what Jesus did not say.
Jesus addressed Peter's future instead of imprisoning him in his past.
The enemy says your story is over.
Jesus says your story is being rewritten.
The enemy says scandal defines you.
This is why our ministry exists under the banner:
But because the cross is greater.
The Gospel is not God pretending sin does not matter.
The Gospel is God paying for sin Himself through Jesus Christ.
When Jesus cried from the cross:
No human effort capable of adding to what Christ already accomplished.
The Hebrew Scriptures had foretold this centuries earlier.
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities.”
The Messiah would be pierced for sinners.
This is why “Follow Me” is not merely a command.
It is an invitation purchased by blood.
Every step behind Jesus was paid for at Calvary.
And perhaps this is the lesson I learned that I will never forget:
Following Jesus is not about becoming impressive.
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.” (Luke 9:23)
He was not calling people into religion.
He was calling them into transformation.
And maybe that is where you find yourself today.
Maybe your story contains chapters you wish nobody knew.
Maybe there are mistakes you cannot undo.
Maybe there are wounds nobody sees.
Maybe there are nights when you wonder if God has given up on you.
Hear the voice of Jesus again.
The same Jesus who called fishermen still calls sinners.
The same Jesus who restored Peter still restores failures.
The same Jesus who conquered death still changes lives.
If this message spoke to your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
What is one area of your life where Jesus is asking you to trust Him more deeply?
Your testimony may become someone else's reason to keep believing.
Because one share can reach a wounded heart.
One testimony can rescue a discouraged believer.
One act of faith can echo into eternity.
And one decision to follow Jesus can change everything.
The most dangerous place is not where you failed—it is where you stop following after you fail.
